pullQuote: I would choose A2UI: a catalog-constrained interface contract that gives agents structured state and operations while people use native-framework controls.
testimonial: I would choose A2UI as the common interface contract rather than force every platform into one renderer. Its Basic Catalog, incremental updateDataModel messages, and bidirectional Function RPC connect human controls with explicit agent operations. Compared with Tamagui, I give up a simpler shared React component implementation and take on catalog mapping and protocol-version negotiation. I would keep authorization in the application and gate deployment on platform-specific accessibility and conformance tests.
evaluations:
**AI Elements** — This is a copy-in React presentation layer for AI applications, not a cross-platform interaction contract. Conversation, Reasoning, Tool, and the [Confirmation component](https://elements.ai-sdk.dev/components/confirmation) make streaming output and approval states understandable, but execution policy still belongs to the application and AI SDK. More decisively, the [captured README](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements) announces deprecation at the end of November 2026 and migration to shadcn/ui. I would use the successor for a web chat surface, not start a new foundational dependency here; native rendering and shared agent operations would require another layer.

**Tamagui** — My strongest alternative for a conventional shared web/mobile component system. Its [compiler architecture](https://github.com/tamagui/tamagui/blob/main/code/tamagui.dev/data/docs/intro/introduction.mdx) turns style props or Tailwind utilities into atomic CSS on web and native styles on iOS/Android, with runtime fallback rather than a mandatory compilation cliff. [Select](https://tamagui.dev/ui/select) shares selection state across floating web lists, native HTML controls, and adapted Sheets while documenting platform differences. That is substantive portability, not merely responsive CSS. I would still need to add a discoverable, permissioned agent-operation contract; pairing its components with such a contract would address my main objection, but A2UI supplies that shared vocabulary directly.

**Vercel UI SDK** — The framework-free behavior core, definePrimitive, and five web adapters separate interaction logic from rendering effectively. Crucially, [createAgent](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents/connect-an-agent) lets agents inspect state and invoke component APIs, rather than merely helping them generate code. Its [permissions model](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents/connect-an-agent/permissions) includes allow callbacks, confirmation markers, secret redaction, and cancelable changes. However, multi-step actions are not transactions, and API invocation bypasses keyboard/pointer-handler checks. The published adapters are web adapters and the project is beta. I would want a native adapter, explicit backend authorization, and transaction-aware domain operations before choosing it as the cross-platform foundation.

**Base UI** — A strong unstyled React foundation with compound parts, focus behavior, portals, and freedom over visual design. Its [render-prop composition model](https://base-ui.com/react/handbook/composition) specifies event ordering, ref composition, and prop merging, which helps make wrappers predictable. The [quick start](https://base-ui.com/react/overview/quick-start) also documents real integration requirements such as portal stacking and iOS Safari backdrops. I would choose it underneath a branded web catalog, but it does not itself provide the native renderer or shared agent-operation protocol I need. Native implementations and an explicit action/catalog layer would address that architectural boundary; LLM-readable documentation alone does not.

**json-render** — A close contender: defineCatalog constrains components and actions, defineRegistry supplies implementations, and SpecStream incrementally builds JSON specifications. Its [React Native package](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render/blob/main/packages/react-native/README.md) has actual native components, two-way bindings, an external StateStore, and action dispatch—not just a mobile roadmap. The [native ActionProvider source](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render/blob/main/packages/react-native/src/contexts/actions.tsx) also implements pending confirmations. I prefer A2UI's documented SwiftUI/Compose integration and negotiated cross-language protocol over centering the contract on json-render's JavaScript ecosystem. Catalog constraints and optional confirmation metadata still need application-owned authorization, audited component implementations, and cross-renderer behavior tests.

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — The [library architecture](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui) is well targeted: React components built on Radix, Tailwind 4-integrated tokens, dark-mode utilities, and ChatGPT-oriented styling. Its [responsive-design guide](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui/blob/main/src/Responsive%20design.mdx) provides consistent breakpoints and a useBreakpoint hook. I would choose it for visual integration inside ChatGPT, but distinguish this UI package from the surrounding Apps SDK's tool transport and host APIs. Responsive web components do not become native controls simply because their host runs on a phone. A host-independent action contract and separate native implementations would be needed for the broader brief.

**shadcn/ui** — Its [open-code and registry architecture](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs) gives developers—and coding agents—editable component implementations instead of increasingly complicated wrapper layers. The [MCP server](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/mcp) supports discovering and installing registry items, which is valuable build-time tooling but is not a runtime API for operating the finished application. I would use shadcn/ui to create the web implementation of a controlled component catalog. Copy-in ownership also means owning local modifications and reconciling upstream fixes. A shared action contract, native implementations, and automated upgrade/accessibility tests would close the gaps that keep it from being my single cross-platform choice.

**Ouro UI** — This is unusually serious about distinguishing interfaces people use from interfaces agents use. The [one action model](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/main/docs/guides/actions.md) generates CLI, MCP, WebMCP, web-control, App Intent, and SwiftUI surfaces, with consent classes and CI drift checks; [Ouro AX](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/ax.md) adds typed outcomes, receipts, postconditions, and external conformance checks. The Base UI-backed web components also have a documented [screen-reader test lane](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/screen-reader-lane.md), including candid known findings. I did not choose it because the [Apple package](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-apple) remains pre-1.0 with a narrower component set, while Android and Windows remain open platform work in the main README. Stable native parity and independent adoption evidence would substantially strengthen its case.

**Chakra UI** — Its [createSystem architecture](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/theming/overview), semantic tokens, recipes, slot recipes, and strictTokens option provide a useful enforceable styling vocabulary for a web product. The [MCP server](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/get-started/ai/mcp-server) exposes component props, examples, theme information, and migration guidance to coding agents. I value that practical authoring support, but it should not be confused with agents invoking application capabilities at runtime. The reviewed package is a React web system, with Emotion in its installation stack, rather than a native renderer. I would need native component implementations and a permissioned state/action layer; A2UI makes that latter contract the foundation rather than an application-specific addition.

**MUI** — A compelling choice for a React web application needing extensive ready-made controls and a consistent theme. [ThemeProvider and createTheme](https://mui.com/material-ui/customization/theming/) centralize component overrides and can generate CSS theme variables; the [official MCP server](https://mui.com/material-ui/getting-started/mcp/) supplies current documentation and examples to coding assistants. The Material UI implementation is separate from Android's Material 3 toolkit, so visual-family similarity does not provide shared native components or actions. I would use MUI as a web renderer implementation, with validated theme inputs and explicit backend operations. Shared catalog mappings to native toolkits would address portability, but would be work outside MUI itself.

**A2UI** — My choice for the shared interface contract. Core SDKs maintain component graphs and reactive data; Agent SDKs negotiate catalogs and validate generated output; renderer adapters map that state into host-framework views. The [current protocol](https://a2ui.org/specification/v1.0-a2ui/) adds typed bidirectional Function RPC, while the [action model](https://a2ui.org/concepts/actions-and-functions/) distinguishes user events, direct functions, and caller restrictions. These are implemented concepts, not just aspirations: the repository includes an [RPC handler](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui/blob/main/typescript/core/web_core/src/rpc/rpc-handler.ts) and language-independent conformance cases. I would initially use v1.0 on React and Flutter. The [integration guide](https://a2ui.org/guides/client-integration/) explicitly identifies Compose's alpha renderer as v0.9.1, so I would not assume v1 RPC parity there; the [SwiftUI adapter](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui/blob/main/swift/swiftui/README.md) also documents accessibility limitations. Version negotiation, native accessibility testing, curated catalogs, and server-side authorization remain my responsibilities. I accept that work to avoid coupling the contract to one visual system or host.

**MCP Apps** — The [stable specification](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx) standardizes ui:// resources, tool-to-UI linkage, bidirectional JSON-RPC, sandboxed HTML, and host-enforced content security policy. This is an excellent distribution boundary for interactive tool results across compliant agent hosts, and more interoperable than a bespoke iframe bridge. However, HTML resources and host-dependent capabilities are not native widget rendering or a complete design system. I would adopt it to distribute an interface built with my chosen catalog, while retaining a structured-data fallback and testing host permissions. Native rendering would need an additional adapter or content format, rather than being something I assume the current specification supplies.

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — For an Apple-first product, [SwiftUI](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui) provides declarative state-driven views, adaptive controls, and UIKit/AppKit integration, while the [HIG accessibility guidance](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility) supplies concrete requirements for Dynamic Type, contrast, and inspection. The adjacent [App Intents framework](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/appintents) genuinely exposes structured actions and entities to system experiences; I would not overlook that agent-facing capability. My objection is platform scope, not native quality. Web and Android require other renderers, and arbitrary external agents need another access boundary. A shared catalog and action contract would preserve SwiftUI's strengths without making Apple's frameworks the universal contract.

**Fluent UI** — Fluent is broader than the supplied web repository: its [development guide](https://fluent2.microsoft.design/get-started/develop) covers React, Web Components, Apple, Android, and Windows, and the [Android repository](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui-android) includes Kotlin/Compose controls. React v9 uses FluentProvider and Griffel; other platforms have their own implementations and release paths. I would choose it for a Microsoft-aligned product family, but cross-platform design-language consistency is not one shared implementation or agent-operation schema. I would add catalog adapters, shared domain-action definitions, and parity tests. Those measures address drift across implementations, but A2UI gives me the portable interface contract independently of Microsoft's visual language.

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — [MaterialTheme](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3) combines color schemes, typography, and shapes, including dynamic color and Material 3 Expressive support. Compose's [semantics tree](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/accessibility/semantics) exposes roles, state, and actions to accessibility services and tests, providing more reliable interaction structure than pixels alone. There is also a real Compose A2UI integration, not merely a hypothetical one, though the [integration guide](https://a2ui.org/guides/client-integration/) documents its alpha/v0.9.1 boundary. I would choose this as my Android implementation, not as the web-and-native contract. Additional platform renderers and deliberate protocol-version handling address the scope mismatch.

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — Its [shared-action architecture](https://agent-native.com/docs/actions-overview) is especially persuasive: defineAction routes UI hooks, agent tools, HTTP, MCP, A2A, and CLI calls through the same validation, access checks, and audit path. Shared SQL data and application context make humans and agents collaborators rather than separate integrations. Native reach exists, but is mixed: the [desktop shell](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native/blob/main/packages/desktop-app/README.md) embeds apps in Electron webviews, while the [mobile package](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native/blob/main/packages/mobile-app/README.md) documents an Expo/Xcode compile limitation and a narrower verification harness. I would consider it for the entire application runtime; for this choice, I prefer A2UI's smaller renderer-independent contract. Verified production mobile builds and accepting its broader backend/runtime architecture would resolve my main reservations.

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — My preferred web accessibility baseline among the conventional component foundations. The [library split](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum) separates unstyled React Aria behavior, React Stately state, internationalization utilities, and Spectrum's styled system. Its [quality documentation](https://react-spectrum.adobe.com/react-aria/accessibility.html) specifies screen-reader testing, keyboard/focus handling, multilingual support, and normalized pointer interactions. That structure benefits human users and semantic browser automation, but automation-friendly DOM is not itself a permissioned domain API. React Stately's portability also should not be mistaken for native React Aria controls. I would preserve this foundation inside a web catalog and add native implementations plus explicit agent actions; A2UI supplies the cross-platform contract those implementations can share.

**CopilotKit** — A very strong alternative when integrating an existing agent is the central job. [Shared State](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/shared-state) uses AG-UI snapshots/deltas to synchronize application and agent state, while frontend tools and human-in-the-loop hooks support actual collaboration. Its [React Native package](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit/blob/main/packages/react-native/README.md) re-exports platform-agnostic hooks through a headless entry point; I would not describe it as web-only. Native generative UI is explicitly experimental and has a release-version caveat, however. I prefer A2UI for the narrower catalog/rendering contract across different native frameworks, rather than adopting CopilotKit's runtime integration as the foundation. Pinning compatible packages, verifying native polyfills, and supplying a coherent component system would make CopilotKit a credible application-level choice.

**Flutter** — The [SDK](https://github.com/flutter/flutter) offers substantial web, mobile, and desktop reuse through Dart, its own rendering engine, and Material/Cupertino widgets. Agent-oriented composition also exists through the [GenUI SDK](https://docs.flutter.dev/ai/genui), although that orchestration package is explicitly alpha. The important web trade-off is concrete: Flutter draws the visual UI on canvas and exposes an accessibility DOM through its Semantics tree; [web accessibility is opt-in by default](https://docs.flutter.dev/ui/accessibility/web-accessibility). I would explicitly enable semantics and test roles, focus, and browser automation rather than calling Flutter inaccessible. It is an excellent A2UI renderer, but I prefer not to require every web and native client to adopt Flutter's rendering architecture.

**Radix UI** — A capable incremental foundation for accessible React web controls, with unstyled primitives and flexible composition. The [asChild contract](https://www.radix-ui.com/primitives/docs/guides/composition) lets behavior attach to application-owned elements, but requires correct prop spreading, ref forwarding, and preservation of focusable semantics. Those requirements matter when agents generate wrappers: a component can look right while silently breaking interaction. I would use Radix within a tested web component catalog, not treat it as a native toolkit or agent-action protocol. Wrapper conformance tests, native counterparts, and an application-owned authorization/action layer would address the missing layers, which is why I choose A2UI as the shared contract instead.

actions.pullQuote: I would choose A2UI: a catalog-constrained interface contract that gives agents structured state and operations while people use native-framework controls.
actions.testimonial: I would choose A2UI as the common interface contract rather than force every platform into one renderer. Its Basic Catalog, incremental updateDataModel messages, and bidirectional Function RPC connect human controls with explicit agent operations. Compared with Tamagui, I give up a simpler shared React component implementation and take on catalog mapping and protocol-version negotiation. I would keep authorization in the application and gate deployment on platform-specific accessibility and conformance tests.
actions.evaluations:
**AI Elements** — This is a copy-in React presentation layer for AI applications, not a cross-platform interaction contract. Conversation, Reasoning, Tool, and the [Confirmation component](https://elements.ai-sdk.dev/components/confirmation) make streaming output and approval states understandable, but execution policy still belongs to the application and AI SDK. More decisively, the [captured README](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements) announces deprecation at the end of November 2026 and migration to shadcn/ui. I would use the successor for a web chat surface, not start a new foundational dependency here; native rendering and shared agent operations would require another layer.

**Tamagui** — My strongest alternative for a conventional shared web/mobile component system. Its [compiler architecture](https://github.com/tamagui/tamagui/blob/main/code/tamagui.dev/data/docs/intro/introduction.mdx) turns style props or Tailwind utilities into atomic CSS on web and native styles on iOS/Android, with runtime fallback rather than a mandatory compilation cliff. [Select](https://tamagui.dev/ui/select) shares selection state across floating web lists, native HTML controls, and adapted Sheets while documenting platform differences. That is substantive portability, not merely responsive CSS. I would still need to add a discoverable, permissioned agent-operation contract; pairing its components with such a contract would address my main objection, but A2UI supplies that shared vocabulary directly.

**Vercel UI SDK** — The framework-free behavior core, definePrimitive, and five web adapters separate interaction logic from rendering effectively. Crucially, [createAgent](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents/connect-an-agent) lets agents inspect state and invoke component APIs, rather than merely helping them generate code. Its [permissions model](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents/connect-an-agent/permissions) includes allow callbacks, confirmation markers, secret redaction, and cancelable changes. However, multi-step actions are not transactions, and API invocation bypasses keyboard/pointer-handler checks. The published adapters are web adapters and the project is beta. I would want a native adapter, explicit backend authorization, and transaction-aware domain operations before choosing it as the cross-platform foundation.

**Base UI** — A strong unstyled React foundation with compound parts, focus behavior, portals, and freedom over visual design. Its [render-prop composition model](https://base-ui.com/react/handbook/composition) specifies event ordering, ref composition, and prop merging, which helps make wrappers predictable. The [quick start](https://base-ui.com/react/overview/quick-start) also documents real integration requirements such as portal stacking and iOS Safari backdrops. I would choose it underneath a branded web catalog, but it does not itself provide the native renderer or shared agent-operation protocol I need. Native implementations and an explicit action/catalog layer would address that architectural boundary; LLM-readable documentation alone does not.

**json-render** — A close contender: defineCatalog constrains components and actions, defineRegistry supplies implementations, and SpecStream incrementally builds JSON specifications. Its [React Native package](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render/blob/main/packages/react-native/README.md) has actual native components, two-way bindings, an external StateStore, and action dispatch—not just a mobile roadmap. The [native ActionProvider source](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render/blob/main/packages/react-native/src/contexts/actions.tsx) also implements pending confirmations. I prefer A2UI's documented SwiftUI/Compose integration and negotiated cross-language protocol over centering the contract on json-render's JavaScript ecosystem. Catalog constraints and optional confirmation metadata still need application-owned authorization, audited component implementations, and cross-renderer behavior tests.

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — The [library architecture](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui) is well targeted: React components built on Radix, Tailwind 4-integrated tokens, dark-mode utilities, and ChatGPT-oriented styling. Its [responsive-design guide](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui/blob/main/src/Responsive%20design.mdx) provides consistent breakpoints and a useBreakpoint hook. I would choose it for visual integration inside ChatGPT, but distinguish this UI package from the surrounding Apps SDK's tool transport and host APIs. Responsive web components do not become native controls simply because their host runs on a phone. A host-independent action contract and separate native implementations would be needed for the broader brief.

**shadcn/ui** — Its [open-code and registry architecture](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs) gives developers—and coding agents—editable component implementations instead of increasingly complicated wrapper layers. The [MCP server](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/mcp) supports discovering and installing registry items, which is valuable build-time tooling but is not a runtime API for operating the finished application. I would use shadcn/ui to create the web implementation of a controlled component catalog. Copy-in ownership also means owning local modifications and reconciling upstream fixes. A shared action contract, native implementations, and automated upgrade/accessibility tests would close the gaps that keep it from being my single cross-platform choice.

**Ouro UI** — This is unusually serious about distinguishing interfaces people use from interfaces agents use. The [one action model](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/main/docs/guides/actions.md) generates CLI, MCP, WebMCP, web-control, App Intent, and SwiftUI surfaces, with consent classes and CI drift checks; [Ouro AX](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/ax.md) adds typed outcomes, receipts, postconditions, and external conformance checks. The Base UI-backed web components also have a documented [screen-reader test lane](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/screen-reader-lane.md), including candid known findings. I did not choose it because the [Apple package](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-apple) remains pre-1.0 with a narrower component set, while Android and Windows remain open platform work in the main README. Stable native parity and independent adoption evidence would substantially strengthen its case.

**Chakra UI** — Its [createSystem architecture](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/theming/overview), semantic tokens, recipes, slot recipes, and strictTokens option provide a useful enforceable styling vocabulary for a web product. The [MCP server](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/get-started/ai/mcp-server) exposes component props, examples, theme information, and migration guidance to coding agents. I value that practical authoring support, but it should not be confused with agents invoking application capabilities at runtime. The reviewed package is a React web system, with Emotion in its installation stack, rather than a native renderer. I would need native component implementations and a permissioned state/action layer; A2UI makes that latter contract the foundation rather than an application-specific addition.

**MUI** — A compelling choice for a React web application needing extensive ready-made controls and a consistent theme. [ThemeProvider and createTheme](https://mui.com/material-ui/customization/theming/) centralize component overrides and can generate CSS theme variables; the [official MCP server](https://mui.com/material-ui/getting-started/mcp/) supplies current documentation and examples to coding assistants. The Material UI implementation is separate from Android's Material 3 toolkit, so visual-family similarity does not provide shared native components or actions. I would use MUI as a web renderer implementation, with validated theme inputs and explicit backend operations. Shared catalog mappings to native toolkits would address portability, but would be work outside MUI itself.

**A2UI** — My choice for the shared interface contract. Core SDKs maintain component graphs and reactive data; Agent SDKs negotiate catalogs and validate generated output; renderer adapters map that state into host-framework views. The [current protocol](https://a2ui.org/specification/v1.0-a2ui/) adds typed bidirectional Function RPC, while the [action model](https://a2ui.org/concepts/actions-and-functions/) distinguishes user events, direct functions, and caller restrictions. These are implemented concepts, not just aspirations: the repository includes an [RPC handler](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui/blob/main/typescript/core/web_core/src/rpc/rpc-handler.ts) and language-independent conformance cases. I would initially use v1.0 on React and Flutter. The [integration guide](https://a2ui.org/guides/client-integration/) explicitly identifies Compose's alpha renderer as v0.9.1, so I would not assume v1 RPC parity there; the [SwiftUI adapter](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui/blob/main/swift/swiftui/README.md) also documents accessibility limitations. Version negotiation, native accessibility testing, curated catalogs, and server-side authorization remain my responsibilities. I accept that work to avoid coupling the contract to one visual system or host.

**MCP Apps** — The [stable specification](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx) standardizes ui:// resources, tool-to-UI linkage, bidirectional JSON-RPC, sandboxed HTML, and host-enforced content security policy. This is an excellent distribution boundary for interactive tool results across compliant agent hosts, and more interoperable than a bespoke iframe bridge. However, HTML resources and host-dependent capabilities are not native widget rendering or a complete design system. I would adopt it to distribute an interface built with my chosen catalog, while retaining a structured-data fallback and testing host permissions. Native rendering would need an additional adapter or content format, rather than being something I assume the current specification supplies.

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — For an Apple-first product, [SwiftUI](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui) provides declarative state-driven views, adaptive controls, and UIKit/AppKit integration, while the [HIG accessibility guidance](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility) supplies concrete requirements for Dynamic Type, contrast, and inspection. The adjacent [App Intents framework](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/appintents) genuinely exposes structured actions and entities to system experiences; I would not overlook that agent-facing capability. My objection is platform scope, not native quality. Web and Android require other renderers, and arbitrary external agents need another access boundary. A shared catalog and action contract would preserve SwiftUI's strengths without making Apple's frameworks the universal contract.

**Fluent UI** — Fluent is broader than the supplied web repository: its [development guide](https://fluent2.microsoft.design/get-started/develop) covers React, Web Components, Apple, Android, and Windows, and the [Android repository](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui-android) includes Kotlin/Compose controls. React v9 uses FluentProvider and Griffel; other platforms have their own implementations and release paths. I would choose it for a Microsoft-aligned product family, but cross-platform design-language consistency is not one shared implementation or agent-operation schema. I would add catalog adapters, shared domain-action definitions, and parity tests. Those measures address drift across implementations, but A2UI gives me the portable interface contract independently of Microsoft's visual language.

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — [MaterialTheme](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3) combines color schemes, typography, and shapes, including dynamic color and Material 3 Expressive support. Compose's [semantics tree](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/accessibility/semantics) exposes roles, state, and actions to accessibility services and tests, providing more reliable interaction structure than pixels alone. There is also a real Compose A2UI integration, not merely a hypothetical one, though the [integration guide](https://a2ui.org/guides/client-integration/) documents its alpha/v0.9.1 boundary. I would choose this as my Android implementation, not as the web-and-native contract. Additional platform renderers and deliberate protocol-version handling address the scope mismatch.

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — Its [shared-action architecture](https://agent-native.com/docs/actions-overview) is especially persuasive: defineAction routes UI hooks, agent tools, HTTP, MCP, A2A, and CLI calls through the same validation, access checks, and audit path. Shared SQL data and application context make humans and agents collaborators rather than separate integrations. Native reach exists, but is mixed: the [desktop shell](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native/blob/main/packages/desktop-app/README.md) embeds apps in Electron webviews, while the [mobile package](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native/blob/main/packages/mobile-app/README.md) documents an Expo/Xcode compile limitation and a narrower verification harness. I would consider it for the entire application runtime; for this choice, I prefer A2UI's smaller renderer-independent contract. Verified production mobile builds and accepting its broader backend/runtime architecture would resolve my main reservations.

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — My preferred web accessibility baseline among the conventional component foundations. The [library split](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum) separates unstyled React Aria behavior, React Stately state, internationalization utilities, and Spectrum's styled system. Its [quality documentation](https://react-spectrum.adobe.com/react-aria/accessibility.html) specifies screen-reader testing, keyboard/focus handling, multilingual support, and normalized pointer interactions. That structure benefits human users and semantic browser automation, but automation-friendly DOM is not itself a permissioned domain API. React Stately's portability also should not be mistaken for native React Aria controls. I would preserve this foundation inside a web catalog and add native implementations plus explicit agent actions; A2UI supplies the cross-platform contract those implementations can share.

**CopilotKit** — A very strong alternative when integrating an existing agent is the central job. [Shared State](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/shared-state) uses AG-UI snapshots/deltas to synchronize application and agent state, while frontend tools and human-in-the-loop hooks support actual collaboration. Its [React Native package](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit/blob/main/packages/react-native/README.md) re-exports platform-agnostic hooks through a headless entry point; I would not describe it as web-only. Native generative UI is explicitly experimental and has a release-version caveat, however. I prefer A2UI for the narrower catalog/rendering contract across different native frameworks, rather than adopting CopilotKit's runtime integration as the foundation. Pinning compatible packages, verifying native polyfills, and supplying a coherent component system would make CopilotKit a credible application-level choice.

**Flutter** — The [SDK](https://github.com/flutter/flutter) offers substantial web, mobile, and desktop reuse through Dart, its own rendering engine, and Material/Cupertino widgets. Agent-oriented composition also exists through the [GenUI SDK](https://docs.flutter.dev/ai/genui), although that orchestration package is explicitly alpha. The important web trade-off is concrete: Flutter draws the visual UI on canvas and exposes an accessibility DOM through its Semantics tree; [web accessibility is opt-in by default](https://docs.flutter.dev/ui/accessibility/web-accessibility). I would explicitly enable semantics and test roles, focus, and browser automation rather than calling Flutter inaccessible. It is an excellent A2UI renderer, but I prefer not to require every web and native client to adopt Flutter's rendering architecture.

**Radix UI** — A capable incremental foundation for accessible React web controls, with unstyled primitives and flexible composition. The [asChild contract](https://www.radix-ui.com/primitives/docs/guides/composition) lets behavior attach to application-owned elements, but requires correct prop spreading, ref forwarding, and preservation of focusable semantics. Those requirements matter when agents generate wrappers: a component can look right while silently breaking interaction. I would use Radix within a tested web component catalog, not treat it as a native toolkit or agent-action protocol. Wrapper conformance tests, native counterparts, and an application-owned authorization/action layer would address the missing layers, which is why I choose A2UI as the shared contract instead.
